body: Recent scholarship in childhood studies is increasingly directed at decolonizing research on childhood and children’s lives. We not only analyze how normative understandings of childhood produce difference, but we also trouble how spatial categories like the ‘global South’ essentialize difference and suppress the heterogeneity of childhoods (Abebe and Ofosu-Kusi, 2016; Abebe et al., 2022; Balagopalan 2019; De Castro 2020). This dialectic between normative childhood and its ‘other’ has been traced to how racialized thinking served as an organizing principle within colonialism (Cooper and Stoler 1997). Following this, I share how recent debates on global legal justice help us explore the racialized temporality of normative theorizing and then briefly focus on ‘age’ as a critical vector for the working out of racialized assumptions of protection and capacity. I conclude by offering some suggestions around how this racialized evaluative structure of linear time organizes broader efforts that temporally ‘other’ marginalized children in the present.

The recognition of childhood as a temporal phenomenon underpins Childhood Studies. Our multi-disciplinary focus on children as ‘beings’ rather than ‘becomings’ pushes against linear time that the child figure epitomizes. In addition, by opening up the ‘time discipline’ of schooling as that which fails to contend with structural inequities - including the lack of access to basic resources like water, food, healthcare and gendered responsibilities around carework - research has powerfully documented how racialized temporal assumptions that underlie schooling centrally shape children’s everyday material and social realities (Maithreyi and Kannan, 2022; Rajan 2022).

In terms of a specific focus on developmental time as always linear, Claudia Castaneda’s (2002) efforts to problematize the ‘insistent potentiality’ of the child figure as well as Erica Burman’s (2019) theorization of ‘child as method’ are framings that alert us to how normative imaginaries of child development get reproduced within national and global development. This resonates with how early childhood education researchers have critically interrogated linear and sequential stages of child development (Canella and Viruru, 2006; Tesar et al., 2016) as well as ties to Edelman’s (2004) critique of how our social consensus reinforces the privilege of heteronormativity through ‘reproductive futurism’. In a related vein, historians of childhood have explored how imperial logics around the child, “determined and naturalized lines of inclusion and exclusion within discourses of docility, plasticity, and potential” (Millei, 2021: 64) thereby helping us unpack the temporal assumptions that shaped colonial policies and practices (Pomfret 2015; Sen 2005). Additionally, Walter Kohan and Karin Murris (2021) theorize ‘childhood’ and ‘time’ as entangled concepts and discuss how the relationship to time cultivated in educational institutions is linked to colonialism and capitalism. More recently, Camila da Rosa Ribeiro and Zsuzsa Millei (2023) have pithily summed up these effects through a focus on ‘the model of modern childhood’. They state how, “reformers and policy makers have used and still rely on this model today in their civilizing efforts” (p. 135). Drawing from these theorizations while also pushing for a more forthright recognition of linear temporality itself as a constitutively racialized phenomenon, this editorial discusses how this racialization was tied to processes of temporal ‘ordering' that continue to dominantly shape and legitimize present practices of temporal ‘othering'. Research in childhood studies is increasingly attentive to the ethnocentrism of western modernity. Postcolonial and decolonial efforts to unpack this ethnocentrism have constructed linear temporality as a manifestation of epistemic and ontological hierarchies set in place by histories of slavery and colonial violence (Bhambra and Holmwood, 2021; Chatterjee 1993; Chakrabarty 2000; Mignolo and Walsh, 2018; Spivak 2004). Their analysis of how historical time got constructed as a measure of cultural difference troubles the hegemonic temporality of modernity as both linear and singular. According to Dipesh Chakrabarty (2000), this linear framing is linked to the underlying assumption of capital as a universal category by which history becomes knowable. This assumption arranges the rest of the world in terms of the differences that mark ‘underdevelopment’ when viewed against this universality of capitalist modernity, thereby naturalizing a narrative of ‘historical transition’. Walter Mignolo and Katherine Walsh (2018) discuss how the colonization of time is entangled in the colonization of space with the ‘rhetoric of modernity’ working to both invent and regenerate, ‘the world as it presumably is’. This world as it is, is a world in which this linear time of modernity is viewed as paradigmatic, with all ‘non-modern societies’ required to mark their ‘progress’ by adhering to this predetermined trajectory. Not only were epistemic and material hierarchies produced through its linear logic but this racialized trajectory got reinscribed through a binary framing that naturalized western modern knowledge as universal while the rest of the world was viewed as incapable of producing knowledge that was generalizable. Interestingly, recent efforts to reframe debates on global justice draw on the above theorizations to problematize the construction of western/linear time as ‘empty’. Broader research on time as ‘racialized’ (Al-Saiji 2021) and ‘white’ (Mill, 2014) employ decolonial and postcolonial theorizations to critically interrogate the unstated racialized epistemic privilege embedded in linear time. Katherine Hunfield’s (2022) focus on the ‘coloniality of time’ analyzes western epistemic arrogance in the temporal assumptions and certainties that underlie framings of global justice. She reasserts the argument that, “linear historical and naturalized evolutionary time lend themselves to relegating non-Western peoples to the time of ‘catching up’” (Hunfield, 2022: 105). Her work draws on the philosopher Charles Mill (2014) theorizations of linear temporality as ‘White time’. Mill’s attempts are centered around unpacking western normative theory, including its basis in a social contract that is white and exclusionary.
